paras: The threatened lynching at Cedar Rapids, Iowa, took place on March 2, 1882, when an excited mob set out to lynch a gambler accused of shooting saloon keeper Josh Fuller. The accused was hurried to jail before the mob could act, and the episode survives only as a brief wire item that names no one's race.
Fuller kept a saloon at Cedar Rapids, and on March 2 he put a man described as "a drunken gambler" out of doors.

According to the wire report, the man turned and fired through the saloon window, hitting Fuller in the right side of the head and slightly injuring another man. An "excited mob" then "determined to lynch him," but "the would-be murderer was hurried to jail in time to save his neck." The report does not say who took him to jail, how large the mob was, or where it gathered.
The coverage does not show whether Fuller survived, and no report of an inquest, indictment or trial was found. The gambler is never named, and no further mob action is reported.

The story reached the press as one short item in a column of national wire briefs headed "Personal and General," which the Grenada Sentinel of Grenada, Mississippi, printed on March 11, 1882. The same column, with the item word for word, ran that day in the Patron of Husbandry of Columbus, Mississippi. The brief gave the item no headline of its own, called the accused "the would-be murderer," and treated the mob as a passing detail without comment. It gave no race for the gambler, Fuller or the mob, and no Iowa paper's account of the incident was found.

reader.title: Threatened lynching at Cedar Rapids, Iowa (1882)
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
bases: A mob was reported to have 'determined to lynch' a man accused of shooting a saloon keeper, but he was taken to jail first, so this was a threatened lynching [A1].

The only report says the accused gambler was hurried to jail in time to save his neck, so no one was killed by the mob; the 'excited mob' was never counted and the shooting was its stated reason [A1].
One wire brief carries the story [A1]; the only other copy found is the same wire column in another Mississippi paper, not an independent report [A2].

accounts.label: Wire report
accounts.gist: A drunken gambler, put out of Fuller's saloon, fired through the window, hitting Fuller and slightly injuring another man; he was hurried to jail ahead of an excited mob determined to lynch him.

framing.detail: Run without a headline in a 'Personal and General' column of wire briefs; the accused is 'the would-be murderer' and the mob is 'excited', with no comment on it.

record_check.dossier: Fuller was the shooting victim; the person the mob threatened was the unnamed gambler, whose name the coverage does not give
No race is stated for the gambler, Fuller or anyone else; nothing in the text marks this as anti-Black violence

record_check.record: accused of shooting saloon keeper Josh Fuller
record_check.dossier: Supported: accused of shooting Fuller through a window after being put out of the saloon, also slightly injuring another man
He was being taken to jail when the mob formed; the mob never got him
A second Mississippi paper carried the same wire column the same day

info: March 2, 1882 (date of the shooting; the mob threat followed right after)
An unnamed 'drunken gambler' was the target of the threatened lynching; Josh Fuller, the saloon keeper, was the shooting victim; another man was slightly injured
Accused of shooting saloon keeper Josh Fuller through the right side of the head by firing through a window after being put out of the saloon
The accused reached jail 'in time to save his neck'; whether Fuller survived is not stated
